newsitem.title: FRANCE: France still wants European in key NATO command.
newsitem.headline: France still wants European in key NATO command.

text.p: France said on Thursday Spain's move towards full integration into NATO's military command would not deter it from its drive to entrust the alliance's Southern Command to a European officer instead of an American.

"France is not alone on this issue. The idea of a European defence identity is a European position, and France and Spain are on the same wave-length on this matter," Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said.
"France's position is well known" on its desire for a European in the key alliance command, Doutriaux told Reuters in a telephone interview.
The United States has ruled out such an appointment, noting that NATO's chief asset in the region was the U.S. Sixth Fleet.

"We want our Sixth Fleet (based in Italy) under command of an American. It's a very important issue for us. I don't see any room for compromise," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday.
U.S. officials, however, have played down any differences with France, suggesting that Washington was open to a greater role for Europeans lower down in the command structure.
At the urging of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, the Spanish parliament on Thursday endorsed Madrid's full integration in NATO's military command.
Parliamentary backing allows the government to negotiate Spain's position in the 16-member alliance.
Under former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, Spain joined NATO in 1982 but froze integration into the military wing pending a referendum on continued membership.
The referendum, held in 1986, passed with a 52 percent majority but Gonzalez vowed Spain would stay outside NATO's military command structure.
He also pledged that Spain would remain free of nuclear weapons, a condition also attached to Thursday's resolution.

Aznar, who took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule, argued that circumstances had changed due to the end of the Cold War and an alliance decision this year to allow European allies to use NATO equipment and resources for their own operations.
France, which pulled out of NATO's integrated command structure in the 1960s, is proposing to rejoin but has insisted as a precondition that the Southern Command be set aside for a European.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette discussed the matter during a working dinner in Paris on Wednesday, officials said.
Christopher was in Paris for a conference on Bosnia.
